podcast.title: Founding (July 4, 1959)
podcast.body: Island Records was founded on July 4th, 1959, by Englishman Chris Blackwell and two partners in Jamaica. The label's name was inspired by the Harry Belafonte song "Island in the Sun," and it began with a startup capital of 100 pounds. "So on July 4th, 1959, he and two partners created Island Records, taking the name from the Harry Belafonte song Island in the Sun."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Founding and Early Success (1959)
podcast.body: Chris Blackwell founded Island Records in 1959 using his parents' money, with the goal of promoting Jamaican culture to the world. The label quickly achieved a Jamaican number one hit with Level Lackin's "Boogie in My Bones." "He started his own label, Island Records, in 1959, using his parents' money, and had soon produced the Jamaican number one, Boogie and My Bones by Level Lakekin."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Founding and Early Support (1959)
podcast.body: Founded in 1959 by Chris Blackwell, a wealthy Brit who grew up in Jamaica, Island Records was sustained in its early, less profitable years by considerable financial backing from Blackwell's parents. "Chris Blackwell, a wealthy white guy who started his own record label, Island Records in 1959. Blackwell is a Brit who grew up in Jamaica, and with quite a bit of financial support from Mom and Dad, was able to keep Island records afloat when it wasn't bringing in too much money."

podcast.title: Move to England & Diversification (1962)
podcast.body: Although the company was based in the United States after 1962, Chris Blackwell moved back to England that same year and began signing local acts. This expanded Island's roster to include British groups like the Spencer Davis Group, Roxy Music, King Crimson, and Traffic. "That same year, Blackwell moved back to England where he started signing local acts, the Spencer Davis group, Roxy Music, King Crimson, Traffic."

podcast.title: Acquisition of Stiff Records (1983)
podcast.body: Island Records acquired Stiff Records in 1983. Stiff Records, known for its punk releases, was sold off due to irresponsible business practices and bleeding money. "Island Records. One more for this episode, Rough Trade. In 1976, Jeff Travis took a trip across the US buying up all kinds of records and when he got home he didn't have anywhere to put them so he decided to start up a store with his record collection acting as inventory."

podcast.title: Acquisition by Polygram (1989)
podcast.body: Island Records was bought by Polygram in 1989. Polygram eventually morphed into Universal, which is now one of the three major record labels. This acquisition transformed Island from an independent label into a major label entity. "Island was bought by Polygram in 1989, which eventually morphed into Universal, one of today's three major labels."

podcast.title: Signing Pulp (1992)
podcast.body: Island Records signed Pulp in 1992, after being acquired by Polygram, as part of a concerted effort to find new artists. "lo consiguen meter en Island Records."

podcast.title: Chris Blackwell Visit to Jamaica (1996)
podcast.body: Chris Blackwell, the head of Island Records, was a passenger on Jimmy Buffett's plane, "Hemisphere Dancer," when it was mistakenly fired upon by Jamaican police at Negril airport on January 16, 1996. He was visiting his estate in Jamaica alongside Bono and his family. "Bono and his family and some friends including Jimmy Buffett and Island Records head Chris Blackwell visited Blackwell State in Jamaica."

podcast.title: Initial Skepticism for Mumford & Sons (2008)
podcast.body: In early 2008, an unnamed executive at Island Records expressed significant doubt about signing Mumford & Sons, dismissing them as a "banjo band" and "dustbin merchants" and questioning their potential as "the next big alternative band" due to their unconventional instrumentation. "Good Lord Smith. This is 2008. We need the next big alternative band."

podcast.body: Island Records, a prominent independent label in the United Kingdom, was acquired by Polygram as part of its strategy to bolster its roster and find new stars in the early 1990s. "Polygram compró dos de las que posiblemente eran las discográficas independientes más importantes del Reino Unido entre ellas, Island Records."

podcast.title: Acquisition by Universal Music Corporate
podcast.body: Over its operational history, Island Records was acquired by several larger record companies, ultimately becoming a part of the vast "monster" known as Universal Music Corporate. This acquisition complicated existing rights disputes, as Universal Music inherited Island's stake in King Crimson's material. "Islan Records... acaba en el monstruo de Universal Music Corporate."

podcast.title: Chris Blackwell and Bob Marley's Final Flight
podcast.body: Chris Blackwell, the head of Island Records, was asked by Bob Marley to arrange a flight home to Jamaica in his final days. "He asked his friend and head of island records Chris Blackwell to fly him home."

podcast.title: Discovery of The Cranberries
podcast.body: Island Records was the label that discovered The Cranberries, indicating their role in bringing the alternative band to wider attention. "los descubrieron Islan Records."

podcast.title: Distribution of Millie Small's "My Boy Lollipop"
podcast.body: Island Records, a new label founded by Chris Blackwell, was responsible for distributing Millie Small's worldwide hit "My Boy Lollipop." This release was pivotal in breaking Ska music into the mainstream and reaching a global audience. "The big breakthrough was a worldwide hit by Millie Small, called My Boy Lollipop, produced by Englishman Chris Blackwell, and distributed through his brand new Idle and Records label."

podcast.title: Early King Crimson Signings
podcast.body: Island Records signed King Crimson's initial albums, playing a crucial role in the early commercial distribution of the band's work. This relationship later became a source of significant conflict as Robert Fripp discovered the label held more rights to his material than he did. "King Crimson firma sus primeros discos con Island Records."

podcast.title: Financial Advance to My Bloody Valentine
podcast.body: After the costly production of "Loveless," My Bloody Valentine signed with Island Records, which provided them with an advance of half a million dollars. This money was then used to construct a new, ultimately problematic, studio. "Then the band was signed to island records who gave them advance of half a million dollars, all of which was thrown down a rat hole constructing a new studio."

podcast.body: Island Records was a new label run by Englishman Chris Blackwell, which released Desmond Dekker's "The Israelites," Ska's first worldwide hit, in 1969. "Big hits on a new label called Island run by an Englishman named Chris Blackwell."

podcast.title: Independent Label Status in Early 80s
podcast.body: In the early 1980s, Island Records was considered an independent label, notable for releasing music by bands such as U2, who maintained an "indiness" even as they gained popularity. "even U2, who recorded for island records, which in the early 80s was an independent label."

podcast.title: Initial Focus (Jamaican & Caribbean Music)
podcast.body: From its inception, Island Records focused on exporting Ska, Reggae, and other music from Jamaica and the Caribbean to the rest of the world. "from day one, Island Records was all about exporting Scott, Reggae and other music from Jamaica and the Caribbean."

podcast.title: Later Signings
podcast.body: In later years, long after its initial focus on Jamaican music, Island Records expanded its roster to include globally recognized acts such as U2, Nirvana, Melissa Etheridge, and The Cranberries. "Now this was long before Island signed the likes of U2, Nirvana, Melissa Etheridge, the cranberries."

podcast.body: Island Records secured a deal with Florence + The Machine, leading to the release of their debut album, "Lungs," in summer 2009. "she ended up with a deal with island records that resulted in the lungs album in the summer of 2009, very big hit, 3 million copies, plus a couple of prestigious awards."

podcast.title: Lewis Bloom's Persistence and Scouting
podcast.body: Lewis Bloom of the A&R department at Island Records relentlessly scouted Mumford & Sons after their formation in December 2007. He observed them repeatedly until he was confident they were ready for a deal, eventually convincing the label despite initial reservations. "He scouted Mumford and son, surely after the band was formed in December 2007."

podcast.title: Multimedia Collaboration with Philips Media
podcast.body: Island Records partnered with Philips Media to announce "Doors and Windows," a CDI (Compact Disc Interactive) disc by The Cranberries. This release was heralded as a technological breakthrough in multimedia entertainment, offering an interactive look at the band alongside music content. "Island Records and Philips Media announced a technological breakthrough in multimedia entertainment. Doors and Windows, an intimate, interactive look at one of the most successful new groups in music today."

podcast.title: Occasional Self-Recording
podcast.body: While primarily a distributor of existing Jamaican records in the UK, Island Records would occasionally record its own tracks. "The label would occasionally record some tracks of its own, but it made its money from releasing Jamaican records."

podcast.title: Reggae's US Vehicle
podcast.body: Island Records, under Chris Blackwell's leadership, played a crucial role as the primary vehicle for reggae to successfully penetrate the United States market, largely by signing and promoting top Jamaican artists like Jimmy Cliff and Bob Marley and The Wailers. "It was Blackwell in his label that was the vehicle for reggae to break into the United States."

podcast.title: Signing Aggressive Bands
podcast.body: Island Records became active in signing bands from the aggressive music scene, such as Thrice and Thursday, during a period when the music industry as a whole was seeking new sounds beyond the declining pop music trend. "And then that was what kind of when Island came in and signed Thrice in Thursday and this whole like the entire music industry was looking for something else."

podcast.title: UK Distribution Strategy (1960s)
podcast.body: After Chris Blackwell moved back to England, Island Records operated as a distributor of Jamaican records. Blackwell personally hand-sold these records to local shops located in immigrant communities across London, Manchester, and Birmingham. "he moved back to England, where he continued running Island Records, this time as a distributor of Jamaican Records... Blackwell would hand sell to local record shops around immigrant communities, in London, Manchester and Birmingham."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Unconventional Debut Album Deal
podcast.body: Island Records, impressed by the self-financed *Sigh No More* album, negotiated a licensing deal where they licensed the album from Mumford & Sons' indie label, Gentlemen of the Road. Island agreed to cover all manufacturing, distribution, and promotion costs, while the band received only a licensing fee without subsequent profits, deemed the "safest way forward" at the time as it required no upfront money or liability from the band. "Island then negotiated a deal whereby they licensed the album from Mumford through their gentlemen of the road indie label."
